cards.text: New king in Judah, friend. Ahaz son of Jotham takes the throne at twenty years old and reigns in Jerusalem sixteen years. Up north, Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, is in his seventeenth year.

cards.question: Like David his father, King Ahaz does what is right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
King Ahaz doesn't follow the ways of David his father. Whose ways does he walk in instead?

cards.text: And then it gets darker. Ahaz even sacrifices his son in the fire.

cards.question: When Ahaz sacrifices his son in the fire, whose abominations is he following?

answers.text: The nations the LORD drove out

cards.text: He sacrifices and burns incense on the high places, on the hills and under every green tree. Then Rezin, king of Aram, and Pekah, king of Israel, come up to wage war against Jerusalem.

cards.question: Rezin and Pekah besiege King Ahaz and overcome him.

cards.text: Two kings, a whole siege, and they STILL can't overcome him. But at that time Rezin recovers Elath for Aram and drives out the men of Judah.

cards.question: Rezin drives the men of Judah out of Elath. Who does he send in to live there?

cards.text: So Ahaz sends messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Two kings outside his walls, and Ahaz goes over BOTH their heads, friend. That's asking for the manager's manager's MANAGER.

cards.question: In his message to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, what does Ahaz call himself?

cards.text: Then comes the ask: "Come up and save me from the hands of the kings of Aram and Israel, who are rising up against me." Servant AND son, friend? That's not a letter, that's adoption paperwork.

cards.question: Ahaz sends a gift to the king of Assyria along with his message. What is it?

answers.text: Silver and gold from the LORD's house and the palace
Horses and chariots from the royal stables
Bronze and iron from the city armories

cards.text: The king of Assyria responds to him and marches up to Damascus. Friend, NOTHING gets a reply that fast like a message with gold attached.

cards.question: The king of Assyria captures Damascus and puts Rezin to death.
The king of Assyria takes the people of Damascus to ___ as captives.

cards.text: With Damascus captured, King Ahaz goes there to meet Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. And while he's in Damascus, something catches his eye.

cards.question: Something in Damascus catches King Ahaz's eye. What is it?

cards.text: Ahaz sends Uriah the priest a model of the altar and complete plans for building it. That's somebody on vacation texting their contractor a photo and the measurements before they've even unpacked.

cards.question: Uriah the priest finishes building the altar before King Ahaz gets back from Damascus.
King Ahaz comes back from Damascus and sees the new altar. What does he do?

answers.text: Orders Uriah to tear it down
Has it moved into the palace

cards.text: He offers his burnt offering and his grain offering, pours out his drink offering and splatters the blood of his peace offerings on the new altar.

But the bronze altar that stood before the LORD is right out front, between the new altar and the house of the LORD. Old altar, shiny new altar, and friend, I know how this goes, because a shiny new stamper is how I ended up in the junk drawer.

cards.question: What does King Ahaz do with the bronze altar that stood before the LORD?

answers.text: Moves it to the north side of the new altar
Sends it off to the king of Assyria
Breaks it apart and melts down the bronze

cards.text: Then King Ahaz commands Uriah the priest: the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering, the king's offerings and all the people's offerings go on the great altar. All the blood of the burnt offerings and sacrifices gets splattered there too.

cards.question: With every offering going on the great altar, what does Ahaz say he'll use the bronze altar for?

answers.text: To burn incense for the people

cards.question: Uriah the priest pushes back on King Ahaz's commands about the altars.

cards.text: And Ahaz keeps going. He cuts off the frames of the movable stands, removes the bronze basin from each one and takes down the Sea from the bronze oxen that were under it.

cards.question: King Ahaz takes the Sea down off the bronze oxen. Where does he put it?

cards.text: Then he removes the Sabbath canopy they had built in the temple and closes the royal entryway outside the house of the LORD.

cards.question: Why does King Ahaz remove the Sabbath canopy and close the royal entryway?

answers.text: On account of the king of Assyria
To make room for the new altar

cards.text: The rest of Ahaz's acts are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Then Ahaz rests with his fathers and is buried with them in the City of David.

cards.question: After Ahaz is buried in the City of David, his son ___ reigns in his place.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences. Only the opening card may run to 3.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke compares Ahaz's appeal to escalating a complaint to a manager. Ahaz is calling a bigger power to rescue him, not complaining to Rezin and Pekah's boss. Tiglath-pileser isn't over them, so the 'over BOTH their heads' comparison doesn't share the core action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences: the quoted ask, 'Servant AND son, friend?' and the adoption paperwork line.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The line 'NOTHING gets a reply that fast' says the king of Assyria answered quickly. 2 Kings 16:9 gives no timing. The line also says the gold was 'attached' to the message, which v8 leaves open.

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: The right answer is a group of nations, and 'The people of Babylon' is a nation, but 'The prophets of Baal' is a group of prophets. Only the right answer uses 'the LORD,' which makes it stand out as the Bible-sounding choice.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The setup line 'I know how this goes' and the comparison to being replaced and moved into a drawer point the baker toward the old altar being moved aside rather than destroyed or sent away. That hints at the answer to card 8.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer 'On account of the king of Assyria' uses the BSB's Bible-sounding phrasing. The wrong answers are plain modern wording ('To make room for the new altar', 'Because Uriah the priest asked'), so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates stop 2: 6 of its 9 choice cards are multiple choice, 2 are true or false and 1 is fill in the blank. Stop 2 also repeats stop 1's pattern of a single fill in the blank on a name as the last card.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: After card 7, the story cards (9, 12, 14, 16) are plain retelling with no reaction, comparison or disbelief. Several moments could hold a laugh without muddying a fact, such as Ahaz taking apart the temple furnishings piece by piece. Stop 1 cards 4 and 6 are also flat, though the son sacrifice on card 4 rightly carries no joke.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
